title: Elite Universities Are a Cartel: Selling Status, Not Education
dek: America's elite universities are not charitable educational institutions but a cartel that maintains its brand by freezing enrollment, cultivating alumni donations, and securing federal research grants; they sell status, not education.
why: Using an RTS game framework to dissect elite university finances, this episode links endowments, admissions, tenure, and federal grants into a closed loop—a fresh and counterintuitive perspective.
who: Students and parents preparing for U.S. undergraduate applications, education entrepreneurs, investors focused on the U.S. innovation system and university finances, and anyone wanting to understand why elite universities keep getting more expensive.
skip: The software ad at 23:12-25:12 can be skipped.

points.h: High selectivity is not an educational advantage; it's a status business
points.body: The logic of the American free market is that privatization brings competition, competition produces meritocracy, meritocracy drives innovation and lowers prices. But universities are the counterexample: they were never treated as a market, yet they push prices to the highest in the world. Harvard, Stanford, Princeton, and MIT charge six figures a year; applications surge while enrollment has been frozen for decades, deliberately creating scarcity like Hermès or Ferrari. The host admits from his own work experience: Ivy League graduates are not smarter; they often talk more than they do. These schools have never produced data showing better teaching or employment outcomes, so high selectivity has no educational basis—it's a status business.

points.h: Alumni are not a community; they are the school's sales pipeline
points.body: The advancement department is a sales organization dressed in campus spirit, whose goal is to extract as much new money as possible. Every graduate is a potential crop; the wealthier they are, the more closely they are tracked. Alumni reunions, dinners, and annual giving campaigns are essentially free parties that let the school record your career, financial status, and likelihood of donating—no different from a sales team managing leads in Salesforce. Princeton alumni volunteers solicit classmates without pay, achieving the highest donor participation rate in the country; Harvard's Red Book is a database where alumni self-report income and occupation. Schools even hire staff to monitor IPOs, company sales, inheritances, and other liquidity events, because those are the best harvest moments.

points.h: Money lost on teams and dorms pays off in donations decades later
points.body: Elite universities manufacture membership through layers of small groups: Yale's 14 residential colleges, Harvard's 12 houses, Princeton's 11 eating clubs, plus fraternities, sororities, and clubs. Over 90% of Harvard and Princeton undergraduates live on campus for four years; there is one varsity team per 150 students. The Ivy League bans athletic scholarships, and sports programs run at a loss, serving only to create emotional stickiness. These facilities are like 'happiness buildings' in an RTS game: costly, but designed to bind students' character-forming years (ages 18–22) to their alma mater in exchange for donations decades later. Dorms, dining halls, and gyms are all loss-making investments, but only elite schools can afford them because they have few students and concentrated investment.

points.h: In the longest bull market ever, endowments underperformed index funds
points.body: The endowment office's sole task is to grow the money; its fund managers are the highest-paid on campus, often recruited from Wall Street, investing in private equity and venture capital to chase unicorns. About 5% of the endowment's value is withdrawn annually for operations, paid out on schedule regardless of market swings, to smooth bad years. But the biggest irony: even during the longest bull market in history, after fees, nearly all schools underperformed a plain Vanguard index fund—Harvard lost the most. Since undergraduate enrollment is frozen, tuition is a loss leader; endowments cover about two-thirds of these universities' annual operating budgets. And most endowment money is restricted; only small annual gifts are unrestricted, so schools still work hard to maintain alumni relations.

points.h: When a provost moves one faculty slot, a department gets a death sentence
points.body: The real operator of a university is the provost, who decides departmental budgets and staffing. The strongest unit is the professor: after a six-year probationary period, they face a tenure review; once granted, the school pays their salary forever and can almost never fire them. A single tenure line can cost tens of millions over its lifetime, so schools allocate positions as carefully as an RTS player manages population cap. The provost's most important decision is moving a slot from one department to another; the department that loses the slot is effectively sentenced to death, losing talent, while the winner gets a virtuous cycle. That's why computer science booms while humanities shrink. Nuclear engineering is the counterexample: it was celebrated in the 1970s, and after Chernobyl, schools spent decades paying salaries for an obsolete department.

points.h: Universities are not temples of thought; they are outposts of federal industrial policy
points.body: University research almost always loses money, but it is the core of the U.S. innovation system. Corporations abandoned long-cycle research long ago; universities are the only institutions willing to wait 20 years rather than demand financial returns. The technology behind COVID vaccines came from UPenn, PageRank and optogenetics from Stanford, open-source cryptography from MIT. The federal government reimburses research costs with tax money, universities publish for free, and private companies productize and sell it back to taxpayers at high prices. The government uses grants to steer universities toward national priorities—after the NIH budget doubled in the late 1990s, schools frantically built buildings and hired faculty. So universities are not independent sanctuaries of thought but outposts of federal industrial policy; cutting federal funding would instantly destroy the entire business model.

points.h: Harvard has the most money but is paralyzed by its twelve schools
points.body: Princeton takes a narrow path: no medical school, law school, or business school; it approaches biomedicine through quantitative theory, spending only one-fifth of Harvard's research budget yet staying competitive across fields. Its buildings are almost entirely funded by alumni donations, such as the $100 million energy center and the $180 million neuroscience institute. MIT is the opposite: flush with cash, it spent $400 million on a nanofabrication facility before selling naming rights, filled new buildings with its own Nobel laureates, and in 2025 spun off federally funded fusion research into a for-profit company. Harvard, however, has twelve schools each managing their own budgets and endowments; funds cannot legally be transferred, and its $1.4 billion across-the-river campus sat unfinished for six years after the financial crisis. The decentralized structure makes Harvard's strategic moves extremely slow.

points.h: Challengers can't fight a full-scale war; they must bet on a single discipline
points.body: Top brands tower over all departments; when a new field emerges, stars, donors, and applicants flock to Harvard and Stanford on day one. Lower-ranked schools cannot fight a full-scale war, so they bet on a single area to gain reputation: Babson bets on entrepreneurship, Johns Hopkins on medicine, Carnegie Mellon on CS and robotics, NYU on Stern and Tisch. Meanwhile, undergraduate scarcity is the fuel of the brand; the admissions office's only goal is to maintain the 'can't get in' scarcity, with admissions officers guarding empty counters like Hermès clerks. Early decision (ED) forces students to commit, artificially inflating yield, letting schools win on 'first-choice' rankings.

quotes.text: There is something absurd about charging people nearly half a million dollars in cash for a piece of paper and then asking them to donate out of gratitude for the 4-year experience they paid for.
Their job is to whine and dine each of these individuals into upping their donations to six and seven figures.

This is why no student ever really meets or interacts with the college president. They'll give an occasional speech or pen a letter, but all their time is dedicated to closing the whales rather than the unripe undergrads who are decades away from writing a check.
Yet the twist is that the most reliable donors are not the whales, but instead the students who could never have afforded to attend.
After fees and on net returns, nearly every school has underperformed a run-of-the-mill Vanguard index fund, and no one has lost out on more than Harvard.
Donor restrictions are binding contracts that are enforcable for centuries by the donor's heirs and state attorneys.
Every year at a lesser school is another year wasted, and by the end, you'll have lost decades idling when you could otherwise have been doing your best work.
